analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income and payroll taxes with a 23% national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: The Fair Tax Act of 2009, backed by 65 House cosponsors, never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, payroll taxes, and estate tax, and replace them with a 23% national sales tax on nearly everything people buy [S2]. Every family would get a monthly rebate covering the sales tax up to the poverty level [S2]. The IRS would be defunded, with states collecting the tax instead [S2]. The tax would shut off automatically if the constitutional amendment allowing income taxes were not repealed within seven years [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains go to households with the most wealth: the bill repeals the estate tax entirely and imposes no tax on capital gains, dividends, interest, or any other income from savings and investments, since only consumption is taxed [S2][S3]. High earners who save much of their income would stop paying income tax on what they don't spend. Working families get relief from payroll taxes and a monthly rebate that offsets the sales tax on poverty-level spending [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax [S2].

Provides a monthly 'family consumption allowance' rebate to every registered family equal to the sales tax on the poverty-level budget for that family size, administered through the Social Security Administration [S2][S3].

Sets the national sales tax at 23% of gross payments starting in 2011, exempts business, investment, and export purchases, and lets states with existing sales taxes collect the federal tax for a 0.25% administration fee [S2][S3].
Prohibits funding the IRS after fiscal year 2013 and creates a Sales Tax Bureau and Excise Tax Bureau in the Treasury [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Households that spend most or all of their income — typically middle- and lower-income families — would pay the 23% tax on everything they buy above the rebated poverty level [S2]. Because wealth held in stocks, bonds, and property is taxed only when spent, existing large fortunes would largely escape tax on their accumulated value, and the estate tax on multimillion-dollar inheritances would disappear [S2]. Revenue for Social Security and Medicare would shift from dedicated payroll taxes to annual congressional appropriations from sales tax revenue [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Households that spend most of their income

drawbacks.text: Because it taxes spending rather than income, the burden falls proportionally harder on families that must spend most of what they earn; the poverty-level rebate offsets the tax only on basic consumption, not on spending above it [S2][S3].

The estate tax repeal and the exemption of all investment and business purchases mean accumulated wealth and income from capital go untaxed, shifting a larger share of the total tax load onto wage earners who consume [S2][S3].

The bill terminates its own sales tax if the Sixteenth Amendment is not repealed within seven years — but Congress cannot repeal a constitutional amendment by passing a law, so the bill as written would eventually leave the government with neither an income tax nor the replacement sales tax [S2].
Social Security and Medicare would lose their dedicated payroll tax funding and instead depend on sales tax revenue allocated by the Treasury each year [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real simplification — no income tax filing — and the rebate genuinely protects poverty-level spending. But its core trade is a shift of taxation away from wealth and capital income and onto consumption, and the wealthiest households, who spend the smallest share of what they own, come out far ahead. Independent analyses widely concluded the 23% rate as written would not raise as much money as the taxes it replaces, and the bill's own seven-year sunset (which no Congress could legally execute) leaves the revenue question unresolved. As drafted, it is a large tax cut for the top of the distribution financed by a higher tax on everyday purchases.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which took no action on it, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Linder introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2009 on January 6, 2009, the first day of the new Congress [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the bill's recorded history ends with the referral [S5].
It gathered 65 cosponsors — 64 House Republicans and 1 House Democrat — but that support never translated into committee or floor action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing tax system stayed intact — including income tax rates on capital gains and the estate tax on large inheritances — and the tax preparation and compliance industry kept its market. No group gained material benefits from the bill's death; the outcome simply preserved the status quo distribution of taxes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax system stayed in place

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 64 of the 65 cosponsors were House Republicans, with a single House Democrat, and no vote was ever held in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate tax and taxes no capital gains, dividends, or investment income — only consumption. Because the wealthiest households spend the smallest share of their wealth, the shift moves a large share of the total tax burden onto families that live on their wages.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax compliance industry
industries.note: Abolishing the income tax and defunding the IRS would eliminate the market for tax filing, software, and compliance services. The industry's interest lay in the bill's failure, which preserved the income tax system.

industries.industry: Retailers and sellers of goods and services
industries.note: Sellers would register with tax authorities, collect and remit the 23% tax, and maintain segregated accounts, but would receive an administrative credit of the greater of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted in compensation [S3].
States with existing sales taxes would collect the federal tax and keep a 0.25% administration fee, expanding their role in federal tax administration.
